I have the numbers for the hearing. Do you want the long version or the short one?
The short one, please. The committee will not read a hundred pages.
Okay. The port handles roughly a third of the state's exports, and traffic has doubled in ten years.
Good. And how many users answered the survey?
Just over two thousand. A majority said the service has improved, but only a few said the tariff is fair.
So we have strong evidence on quality, and very little on price.
Exactly. And be careful: the tariff rose by two percentage points, not two percent.
Good point. A mistake like that could destroy our credibility at the hearing.
Just over two thousand users answered the survey.

Most committees are not afraid of numbers. They are afraid of too many numbers. So here are my three rules. First, round your numbers. Nobody remembers thirty-three point seven percent, but everybody remembers roughly a third. Second, every number needs a comparison. Two million users means nothing alone. Two million users, double the number of five years ago, tells a story. Third, one number per slide. If you show twelve numbers, the audience will remember none of them. And please, never say a few when you mean few. The first is good news. The second is bad news.

I have been an expert witness in more than sixty cases, and I see the same mistakes again and again. In one case, a lawyer presented a survey that showed that eighty percent of users were unhappy. It sounded strong. But the sample was only forty people, all from one neighborhood. In another case, the other side said that the tariff had gone up by fifty percent. That was true, but it went from two percent to three percent of the average income: one percentage point. Very little evidence, a lot of drama. My advice to lawyers is simple. Always ask two questions: how big is the sample, and compared with what?

A new study on infrastructure investment has bad news for the region. Most countries invest roughly two percent of their GDP in infrastructure every year, and some invest just under that. According to the authors, they should invest around five percent to close the gap. Private investors are part of the solution, but only a fraction of their money goes to roads, ports and water. A majority goes to energy and telecommunications. The trend is positive, the report says: private investment has doubled in the last ten years. But at the current speed, it will take decades to close the gap.
